Noise cancelling headphones work by listening to the world around you and then playing the opposite sound. Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup pick up steady noise, like the hum of an airplane engine. A chip inside the headphones flips that sound wave upside down, so when the two waves meet, they mostly cancel each other out. This works best for low, constant sounds, which is why you can still hear voices and sudden noises fairly clearly. It's also why the effect can feel a little strange at first, almost like a gentle pressure in your ears.

The train was already moving when Anna reached the platform, her bag bouncing against her hip. She ran anyway, past the empty benches and the flickering clock, until the last door was only a few steps away. A man inside saw her, hesitated, and then pressed the button just in time. The doors slid open with a tired sigh. She jumped in, out of breath, and laughed before she could stop herself. She said thank you, and he only shrugged, as if he did this every morning. Outside, the city slipped away, gray and quiet, and for the first time that week, she felt like she was exactly on time.
